title: Stress Tests: Finding Where the Deal Breaks Before the Market Does
summary: A pro forma tells you what happens if you are right. A stress test tells you what happens if you are wrong, how wrong you can be before the deal breaks, and what you will do when the warning lights come on. Learn the four tools: sensitivities shown as a tornado chart, break-evens, scenarios and triggers.
body:
A pro forma answers one question: what happens if every assumption is right. A stress test answers the questions that decide whether you survive: which assumption matters most, how far it can move before the deal breaks, what happens when several move together, and what you will do the moment one of them starts to move.

Recall

Q. What is the break-even exchange rate in a currency stress?

A. The exchange rate at which debt service coverage falls to 1.0, so income exactly covers debt service.

Q. What is the binding limit when sizing a project loan?

A. The sizing test, such as coverage or loan to cost, that produces the smallest loan and therefore sets the amount the lender offers.

Q. What is debt yield?

A. Net operating income divided by the loan amount. Lenders use it because it does not depend on the interest rate or on a cap rate, so it shows how much income stands behind each dollar of debt.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, you spent years in power-grid operations, where the system is planned to survive the loss of its largest single element and operators rehearse what they will do when a line trips. Development needs the same discipline and rarely gets it. Most pro formas show one column. Lenders, investors and credit committees increasingly ask for the other columns, and a developer who brings them first, with actions attached, is trusted with more money. Every stress test this week uses hypothetical round numbers.

Tool one: sensitivity and the tornado chart

In plain English: move one assumption at a time, by a sensible amount in each direction, and see how much the answer moves.

The professional framing is sensitivity analysis, usually displayed as a tornado chart: a bar chart with one horizontal bar per assumption, each bar showing how far the result swings when that assumption moves up and down, sorted with the widest bar at the top. The shape looks like a funnel, which is where the name comes from. The chart answers the first question: which assumption matters most.

A worked example. A development costs 50,000,000 dollars and is expected to earn stabilised net operating income (NOI) of 4,000,000 dollars, sold at a 6.5 percent capitalisation rate. Value is 4,000,000 divided by 0.065, about 61,540,000 dollars, so profit is about 11,540,000 dollars. Now move one input at a time. Cost plus or minus 10 percent moves profit by 5,000,000 dollars either way. The exit capitalisation rate plus 0.5 percentage points, to 7 percent, cuts value to about 57,140,000 dollars and profit by about 4,400,000; minus 0.5 points, to 6 percent, adds about 5,130,000. NOI plus or minus 5 percent moves profit by about 3,080,000 either way. The tornado shows cost and exit cap rate at the top, NOI below. Your diligence effort should follow the chart: the widest bars deserve the most work.

Tool two: the break-even

In plain English: find exactly how wrong an assumption can be before something you care about fails.

A break-even is the value of one input at which a chosen test is met exactly: profit equals zero, coverage equals 1.0, or the loan reaches its covenant limit. In the example, profit reaches zero when value equals cost, 50,000,000 dollars. Holding NOI at 4,000,000, that happens at a capitalisation rate of 4,000,000 divided by 50,000,000, which is 8 percent. The exit cap rate can rise 1.5 percentage points from 6.5 before the profit is gone. That single number is more useful in a lender meeting than any page of the pro forma.

Say that out loud now.

Which input matters most, how far can it move, and what happens when several move together.

Tool three: scenarios

Sensitivities move one input at a time. Real trouble moves several together, because they share a cause. A recession lowers rents, raises vacancy and widens cap rates in the same year. A scenario is a coherent story with every input set to fit it. Practitioners usually run three: a base case, the plan; a downside case, a plausible bad year; and a severe case, a harsh but realistic combination, the kind that happens once or twice in a career. The severe case is not a prediction. It is a test of survival.

A second worked example, using the same project. Downside: NOI 5 percent lower, cap rate 0.5 points higher, cost 5 percent higher. Value is 3,800,000 divided by 0.07, about 54,290,000 dollars, against cost of 52,500,000, so profit is about 1,790,000 dollars. Severe: NOI 10 percent lower, cap rate 1 point higher, cost 10 percent higher. Value is 3,600,000 divided by 0.075, 48,000,000 dollars, against cost of 55,000,000, a loss of 7,000,000 dollars. The base case promised 11,540,000. The severe case asks whether your equity, your guarantees and your lender can absorb a 7,000,000 dollar loss.

Tool four: triggers

A stress test that ends in a report changes nothing. A trigger is a pre-agreed threshold that, when crossed, sets off a pre-agreed action. For example: if the leasing pace falls 20 percent behind plan for two months, cut the remaining marketing budget and offer the agreed concession package; if coverage falls below 1.25, stop discretionary capital spending and inform the lender before the covenant test. Writing the action in advance, while you are calm, is the whole point. Operators call it a playbook. You will recognise it from operating procedures that tell a control room what to do when a threshold alarm sounds.

Two rules make triggers work. Each trigger needs an owner, a named person who must act, not a committee that must meet. And each trigger must sit above the lender's own threshold, so that you act before the loan agreement acts on you. A trigger at the same level as the lender's cash trap is not a warning; it is a notice that the warning has already passed.

How the best do it

Well-run lenders and insurers run what is called a reverse stress test: instead of asking what a given scenario does to them, they start from failure and ask what combination of events would cause it, then judge how plausible that combination is. A small developer can copy it in one meeting: write "this project failed" at the top of a page, list the three most likely ways it happened, and check that each has a trigger and an action. It is the pre-mortem from Week 2, with numbers attached.

Six-Lens Check

Tax: losses in a severe case may be usable only against certain income or only by certain owners; verify that against the primary source before you rely on it. Liability: the severe case shows which guarantees would be called and for how much. Banking: share the downside and severe cases with the lender before close; it will run them anyway. Governance: the board should approve the triggers and who may act on them. Estate: a severe case that calls a personal guarantee is an estate event, so the plan should know the exposure. Exit: the break-even exit cap rate tells you how much the market can move before a sale stops paying back cost.

Professional sign-off required: independent cost consultant or valuer, on the ranges used for cost and exit value.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is a stress test built to pass, with ranges chosen so that every case still works. The control is to set the ranges from history and from the lender's own assumptions before you run the model, and to have someone independent review them.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner runs sensitivities one variable at a time and calls the deal robust because no single bar breaks it. The bars break it together.

Callback

In Week 2, Kema and Ford taught the pre-mortem and inversion: imagine the failure, then work out how it happened. A stress test is the pre-mortem made numerical, and a trigger is the after-action review written before the action.

Recap

Sensitivities, shown as a tornado chart, rank the inputs. Break-evens show how far each can move. Scenarios move them together in base, downside and severe cases. Triggers turn the test into action. Set the ranges before you run the model, not after.

Next: Ford, with Roman, on Failure Forensics: Dubai World's 2009 standstill and what happens when the severe case arrives as a combination.
checklist: My model shows a base, a downside and a severe case, each a coherent story.
I have a tornado chart ranking the inputs that matter most.
I know the break-even exit cap rate, rent, vacancy and interest rate.
I set stress ranges from history and lender assumptions before running the model.
I have written triggers, each with a pre-agreed action and an owner.
I know which guarantees the severe case would call, and for how much.
I have run a reverse stress test: three ways this project fails.
An independent reviewer has checked my ranges.
head: Field checklist
speak: A pro forma tells me what happens if I am right. A stress test tells me what happens if I am wrong. Four tools. Sensitivities, shown as a tornado chart, move one input at a time and rank them; in my example, cost and exit cap rate swing profit by about 5,000,000 dollars each, NOI by about 3,000,000. Break-evens show how far one input can move before a test fails: profit disappears if the exit cap rate rises from 6.5 to 8 percent. Scenarios move inputs together, because a recession lowers rent, raises vacancy and widens cap rates at once: my base case earns about 11,500,000 dollars, my severe case loses about 7,000,000. And triggers turn the test into action: a threshold, a pre-agreed response and an owner. I set the ranges from history before I run the model, so the test is built to find the break, not to pass.
terms: Tornado chart — a bar chart ranking inputs by how much each swings a result when moved up and down, widest at the top.
Break-even — the value of one input at which a chosen test, such as zero profit or coverage of 1.0, is met exactly.
Trigger — a pre-agreed threshold that, when crossed, sets off a pre-agreed action by a named owner.

hostile.q: Your severe case loses 7,000,000 dollars. Why should we lend against a project that can lose that much?
hostile.a: Because I would rather show you the severe case than have you build it yourself. It assumes a harsh combination that happens rarely, and in it our equity of 20,000,000 dollars absorbs the loss before your loan is touched. We also have triggers: if leasing falls 20 percent behind plan for two months, we act on concessions and spending, and if coverage approaches 1.25, you hear from us before the test. The question is not whether the project can lose money, it is who loses first and how early we act.

title: Dubai World 2009: When the Severe Case Arrived All at Once
summary: In late November 2009, Dubai World, a state-owned conglomerate whose property arm had built some of the region's best-known projects, asked creditors to accept a standstill on its debt. Property prices, credit and refinancing had failed together. Roman joins Ford to show why a stress test that moves one variable at a time can miss the case that matters.
rule: Rule 44: Test the plan against a severe case that moves price, credit and refinancing together, not one variable at a time, and write down in advance the trigger and the action for each, because the severe case arrives as a combination.
body:
Dubai World's request for a standstill on its debt in late November 2009 showed what happens when prices, buyers' deposits and access to new credit all fail in the same season. Each risk had been considered on its own; no plan survived them together.

Recall

Q. What is a severe case in a stress test?

A. A harsh but realistic combination of bad outcomes, set as one coherent story, used to test survival rather than to predict.

Q. In project finance, what is a completion test?

A. The defined physical and financial conditions that must be met before a sponsor's construction support is released.

Q. What is the difference between fixed and floating rate debt?

A. Fixed rate debt pays an agreed rate for a period; floating rate debt resets periodically with a reference rate plus a margin, so the borrower carries the risk of rates rising unless it hedges.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, Roman joins me because this is a lender's lesson as much as a developer's. The case is large and public, but the mechanism works the same way on a single building. The general facts below are widely reported; I avoid amounts I cannot confirm, and where I describe how a developer of that era typically financed, I describe the pattern, not any one entity's documents.

1. Timeline

Through the mid-2000s, Dubai grew rapidly as a property and tourism centre. Dubai World was a government-owned holding company; its property arm, Nakheel, developed large projects including the Palm Jumeirah. Much of the development was financed with borrowing and with off-plan sales, in which buyers pay deposits and instalments before construction is finished. In 2008, the global credit crisis closed many funding markets and property prices in Dubai fell sharply. In late November 2009, Dubai World announced that it would ask creditors for a standstill, a pause in repayments while it restructured. Markets reacted around the world. In December 2009, support from Abu Dhabi allowed Nakheel to repay an Islamic bond, or sukuk, falling due that month. During 2010 Dubai World agreed a restructuring with its bank creditors.

2. Key decisions

Three kinds of decision mattered. Funding long-term development with shorter-term borrowing that would need to be refinanced. Relying on buyers' instalments to fund construction. And launching more projects while prices were rising, so that the pipeline grew fastest at the top of the cycle.

3. Assumptions

The governing assumption was that refinancing would be available when debts fell due, and that buyers would keep paying. A second was that support from the state would be available without limit. Each assumption was reasonable on its own in a rising market. The defect was that they depended on the same thing: confidence.

4. Incentives

Rising prices rewarded speed. Lenders were encouraged by state ownership and lent on the strength of it. Buyers bought off plan expecting to sell on before completion, so demand partly depended on further price rises, which made the sales themselves a bet on the cycle.

5. Warning signs ignored

Credit markets froze in 2008, more than a year before the standstill. Prices fell. Buyers who had bought to sell on stopped paying when they could not sell. Each signal was public. A trigger written in calmer times, such as stopping new launches when sales pace fell or prices dropped by a set amount, would have fired well before the end of 2009.

Say that out loud now.

The severe case is a combination, and its parts share a cause.

6. Point of no return

For a developer, the point of no return in such a cycle is usually the decision to commit to the next large phase while existing debts still need refinancing. After that, every further fall in confidence hits the existing debt, the new commitments and the buyers' payments at once.

7. Root cause

Roman's reading is that the root cause was a funding structure whose risks were correlated. Price, buyer behaviour and refinancing were each modelled, but they were not modelled as one event with one cause. When confidence fell, all three failed together, and a plan built to survive any one of them did not survive the three.

What it means for a developer

A worked example, with hypothetical round numbers. A developer builds 200 apartments costing 60,000,000 dollars, funded by 20,000,000 dollars of equity, a 25,000,000 dollar construction loan due in three years, and 15,000,000 dollars of buyers' instalments. Separate tests: prices fall 15 percent, survivable; a fifth of buyers default, survivable, because units can be resold; the loan must be refinanced at a higher rate, survivable. Combined: prices fall 30 percent, a third of buyers default because they cannot sell on, resold units fetch 30 percent less, and the lender will not refinance until sales recover. Instalments fall short by about 5,000,000 dollars, resale proceeds fall short by more, and the 25,000,000 dollar loan falls due with no new lender. The developer needs fresh equity at the moment equity is hardest to find.

A second example. The same developer, with written triggers: no second phase until the first phase's loan is refinanced; if monthly sales fall 30 percent below plan for two months, stop new launches and retain cash; refinance a year before maturity, not at it. In the combined case, the developer has one project, not two, a year of runway and cash retained. The loss is painful. It is not fatal.

What the lender saw

Roman adds the lender's view, because it explains why the end came so suddenly. A lender looking at a developer with large refinancing needs in a falling market asks three questions at once. Will the collateral cover the loan if prices keep falling? Will the borrower's other creditors move first? And is any backer certain to step in, and on what terms? When the answers are no, possibly and uncertain, rational lenders stop rolling debt, even to a borrower they have known for years. No single lender has to act unreasonably for the whole funding structure to close. That is why refinancing risk is not a risk you can negotiate away at the time; it is a risk you remove by refinancing early, while the answers are still yes.

The same logic applies to buyers. A buyer who paid a deposit expecting to resell asks whether completion is certain and whether the unit will be worth the remaining price. When both answers weaken, the rational buyer stops paying, and many buyers reach that conclusion in the same month.

The prevention habit

Roman's habit is to ask, for every risk in the register, "what else would be true on the day this happens?" If the answer includes another risk on the list, run them together. Then write one trigger per combined case, with its action and its owner, and review the triggers quarterly.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is a stress test that treats correlated risks as independent, so that each looks survivable alone. The control is a severe case built around a single cause, a credit crunch or a recession, with every input set to fit it.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner relies on a strong backer, a parent company, a partner or a state, as the answer to the severe case. A backer's support is a decision someone else makes on the day, under pressure of its own.

Callback

In Week 41, Priya and LEX taught condo pre-sales, deposits and buyer default. Dubai showed what those mechanics do in a falling market: buyers who bought to sell on stop paying together, and the deposits a lender counted on as committed revenue shrink at the moment the lender is least willing to refinance.

Recap

Dubai World's 2009 standstill came after prices, buyer payments and refinancing failed together, driven by one cause, the loss of confidence. Each risk had looked survivable alone. Rule 44 makes the severe case a combination and puts a written trigger and action beside it.

Next: Sage, on The Money: weighting the cases, sizing reserves to the severe case, and what a stress test is worth.
checklist: My severe case is built around a single cause, with every input set to fit it.
For each risk, I have asked what else would be true on the day it happens.
I do not commit to a new phase while existing debt still needs refinancing.
I plan to refinance well before maturity, not at it.
I have a written trigger for slowing or stopping new launches.
I do not treat a backer's support as a certainty in the severe case.
I know how buyers' deposits behave in a falling market.
I have written Rule 44 in my decision journal.
head: Field checklist
speak: Dubai World was a government-owned holding company whose property arm, Nakheel, built projects including the Palm Jumeirah. Development was funded with borrowing that needed refinancing and with buyers' off-plan instalments. When the 2008 credit crisis hit and prices fell, buyers who had bought to sell on stopped paying, refinancing dried up, and in late November 2009 Dubai World asked its creditors for a standstill. Support from Abu Dhabi let Nakheel repay a sukuk in December 2009, and a restructuring followed in 2010. The root cause was correlated risk: price, buyer behaviour and refinancing each looked survivable alone, but they shared one cause, confidence, and failed together. In my hypothetical example, each test alone was survivable, and combined they left a loan falling due with no lender. Rule 44: test a severe case that moves price, credit and refinancing together, and write the trigger and action for each in advance.
terms: Standstill — an agreement or request that creditors pause repayment demands and enforcement while a debtor restructures.
Off-plan sale — a sale of a unit before it is built, with deposits and instalments paid during construction.
Correlated risks — risks that tend to happen together because they share a cause.

hostile.q: You have tested a price fall, buyer defaults and a refinancing problem separately and survived each. Why do you need more equity?
hostile.a: Because in a downturn those three happen together, not separately. When I run them as one severe case, buyers default because they cannot sell, resold units fetch less, and the construction loan falls due when no lender will refinance. That leaves a gap of several million dollars. The extra equity and the rule to refinance a year before maturity are what close it. Without them we survive every test except the one that actually happens.

title: Weighting the Cases and Sizing Reserves to the Severe One
summary: A probability-weighted result tells you whether a deal is worth doing; the severe case tells you whether you can survive doing it. Learn to compute both, to size liquidity reserves and equity to the severe case, and to see what a stress test is worth in money.
body:
Weighting your cases by probability tells you whether a deal is worth doing. The severe case tells you whether you can survive doing it. You need both numbers, and you size your reserves to the second one, not the first.

Recall

Q. What is Rule 44?

A. Test the plan against a severe case that moves price, credit and refinancing together, not one variable at a time, and write down in advance the trigger and the action for each.

Q. Why does non-recourse debt cost more than recourse debt?

A. Because the lender can look only to the project, so it charges a higher margin, lends less, requires reserves and passes on its diligence costs.

Q. What does loan to cost measure?

A. The loan as a share of total project cost, used by construction lenders to make sure the sponsor has enough equity at risk.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, investors ask two different questions and often blur them. "Is this a good deal?" is answered by the expected outcome. "Can we survive it?" is answered by the severe case. A deal can have an attractive expected profit and still carry a severe case that destroys the sponsor. The skill is to keep the two questions apart and give each its own number.

The expected outcome

In plain English: if you ran this deal many times, what would you earn on average?

The professional framing is the probability-weighted, or expected, outcome: each scenario's result multiplied by the probability you assign to it, then summed. A worked example, with hypothetical round numbers. The base case earns 11,500,000 dollars of profit, with a probability of 60 percent. The downside earns 3,000,000 dollars, probability 30 percent. The severe case loses 8,000,000 dollars, probability 10 percent. Expected profit is 0.6 times 11,500,000, plus 0.3 times 3,000,000, plus 0.1 times minus 8,000,000: 6,900,000 plus 900,000 minus 800,000, which is 7,000,000 dollars. The base case promised 11,500,000. The honest expectation is 7,000,000.

Two cautions. The probabilities are judgments, not data, so treat the expected number as a range and record how you chose the weights. And an expected number of 7,000,000 dollars means nothing to a sponsor who would not exist after the severe case, because you only get to run the deal once.

Survival: sizing to the severe case

In plain English: hold enough cash and equity that the severe case is a bad year, not the end.

The professional framing is to size liquidity and capital to the severe case's cash shortfall over the time it takes to recover. A second worked example, hypothetical. A stabilised building has a 40,000,000 dollar floating rate loan. In the severe case NOI falls to 2,890,000 dollars and debt service rises to 3,800,000 dollars, a shortfall of 910,000 dollars a year. If recovery takes 18 months, the shortfall is about 1,365,000 dollars. Add a cushion for costs that only appear in a crisis, such as leasing commissions and legal fees, say 300,000 dollars, and the reserve to hold is about 1,665,000 dollars, round it to 1,700,000. That number, not the expected profit, decides whether you can hold the building through the bad years without selling at the bottom or handing it to the lender.

Say that out loud now.

The expected case tells me if it is worth doing; the severe case sizes my reserve.

What a stress test is worth

A stress test costs money: an analyst's time, a valuer's review, perhaps a lender's diligence. Its value is the losses it lets you avoid. If the triggers in your plan would have stopped a second phase one year before a downturn, and that second phase would have lost 6,000,000 dollars in the severe case with a 10 percent chance, the expected value of the trigger is 600,000 dollars, before counting the value of surviving at all. A trigger is an option you write yourself: the right to stop, slow or defer when a threshold is crossed. Like any option, it is worth most when uncertainty is greatest.

Reserves also cost money. Cash held in a reserve earns little while your equity's required return may be 15 percent. Holding 1,700,000 dollars costs about 255,000 dollars a year in foregone return at that rate. Compare that with what the reserve protects: the building, your equity and any guarantees that would otherwise be called.

Choosing the weights honestly

Three habits keep the probabilities from becoming wishes. First, set them before you see the results, so the weights cannot be tuned to make the expected profit look attractive. Second, anchor them to history: how often, over the past few decades in this market and this asset type, has a downturn of the downside's size happened in a period as long as your hold? That outside view, which Kema taught in Week 2, is a better starting point than the deal team's mood. Third, write the weights and their reasons in your decision journal. When the deal is finished you can compare what happened with what you assumed, and your next weights will be better.

A useful check is to ask what weight on the severe case would make the expected profit zero. In the example, base and downside together contribute 7,800,000 dollars at their current weights. If the severe case is a loss of 8,000,000, and you scale the other two down in proportion as the severe weight rises, the expected profit reaches zero only when the severe case is given a weight of about 52 percent, more likely than everything else combined. That tells you the deal is attractive on expected terms across a wide range of judgments, which is useful to know before you argue about any single weight.

Value under the cases

Valuers and lenders do the same exercise on value. The base case value at a 6.5 percent capitalisation rate on 4,000,000 dollars of NOI is about 61,500,000 dollars. A severe case of 3,600,000 dollars at 7.5 percent gives 48,000,000 dollars, a fall of about 22 percent. If your loan is 40,000,000 dollars, loan to value moves from 65 percent to about 83 percent. A covenant at 75 percent would be breached in the severe case. That tells you, before close, either to borrow less or to negotiate how a value covenant is cured.

Wealth Ledger

Warrick's note. Run the same three cases on your personal balance sheet. Base: your income, your distributions and your spending as planned. Downside: distributions stop for a year. Severe: distributions stop for two years and one guarantee is called. Your liquidity floor, the cash and near-cash you keep untouched, should cover your spending through the severe case without a forced sale. Many people size their personal reserve to the expected case. Your family lives through the actual case. This is conceptual; a licensed adviser is required before you act.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is quoting the expected profit to investors as if it were the plan, while sizing nothing to the severe case. The control is to report three numbers together: expected outcome, severe-case loss and the reserve held against it.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner sets the probability of the severe case to a number so small that it vanishes from the expected profit, and then treats that as proof it cannot happen. A small probability multiplied by a fatal loss is still fatal on the day it happens.

Callback

In Week 16, Sage taught valuation and appraiser bias, including the gap between as-is and as-complete value. Stress testing adds a third value: as-stressed. A lender who sees all three trusts the first two more.

Recap

Weight the cases to get an expected outcome, and treat it as a range. Size reserves and equity to the severe case's shortfall over the recovery period. Triggers are options you write yourself, and reserves are premiums you pay. Value the asset under the cases to see which covenants would break.

Next: LEX, on The Rules: covenants, cash traps, cures and the triggers lenders write into the loan.
checklist: I compute an expected outcome and record how I chose the weights.
I keep the expected outcome and the severe-case loss as separate numbers.
I size reserves to the severe-case shortfall over the recovery period.
I know what each reserve costs in foregone return.
I value the asset under each case and check every value covenant.
I can state what each trigger is worth as an option.
My personal liquidity floor covers spending through my own severe case.
I report expected outcome, severe loss and reserve together.
head: Field checklist
speak: Two questions, two numbers. Is the deal worth doing? Weight the cases: in my example, 60 percent at 11,500,000 dollars, 30 percent at 3,000,000 and 10 percent at a loss of 8,000,000 gives an expected profit of 7,000,000, not the base case's 11,500,000, and the weights are judgments, so I treat it as a range. Can I survive it? Size to the severe case: if NOI falls to 2,890,000 and debt service rises to 3,800,000, the shortfall is 910,000 dollars a year, about 1,365,000 over 18 months, and with a crisis cushion I hold about 1,700,000. That reserve costs about 255,000 dollars a year in foregone return, which is the premium for not selling at the bottom. I also value the building in the severe case: 48,000,000 dollars, so a 75 percent value covenant would break. A trigger is an option I write myself, and it is worth most when uncertainty is greatest.
terms: Expected outcome — the sum of each scenario's result multiplied by the probability assigned to it.
Liquidity reserve — cash held to cover shortfalls in a downside or severe case without selling assets or defaulting.
Liquidity floor — the minimum cash and near-cash a person or company keeps untouched to survive its severe case.

hostile.q: Your reserve of 1,700,000 dollars cuts our return. Why not distribute it and rely on the expected case?
hostile.a: Because we run this building once, not many times. The expected case says the deal is worth doing; it does not keep us solvent in the severe case. Without the reserve, an 18-month shortfall forces a sale or a default at the worst point in the market, and our equity goes with it. The reserve costs about 255,000 dollars a year in foregone return. I think that is a cheap premium against losing the asset, and I will release it under a written rule once coverage has stayed above an agreed level for a set period.

title: Covenants, Cash Traps and Cures: The Triggers Lenders Write
summary: A lender's stress test lives in the loan agreement as financial covenants and the consequences of breaching them: cash traps, sweeps, events of default and cure rights. Learn to read how each trigger is defined, tested and cured, because the definition often matters more than the number.
body:
A lender writes its own stress test into the loan agreement: financial covenants, a ladder of consequences as they weaken, and limited rights for you to cure. Read the definitions, the testing dates and the cure provisions, because they decide whether a bad quarter is a warning or a default.

Recall

Q. What is a liquidity floor?

A. The minimum cash and near-cash a person or company keeps untouched so it can survive its severe case without forced sales.

Q. What does a direct agreement give a lender?

A. Notice before a key counterparty terminates for the borrower's default, time to cure, and the right to step in and pass the contract to a new owner.

Q. What is a debt service coverage ratio covenant?

A. A loan term requiring net operating income to exceed debt service by a stated multiple, tested on stated dates, with consequences if it is not met.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, two loans with the same covenant number can behave completely differently, because one defines income generously and tests it once a year, and the other defines it strictly and tests it every quarter on trailing figures. Lenders negotiate the definitions with great care. Sponsors often negotiate only the number. I teach concepts and how to think; how any clause is read depends on its wording and on local law, so verify it against the primary source before you rely on it.

Two kinds of financial covenant

In plain English: some covenants are tested all the time, others only when you want to do something.

The professional framing distinguishes maintenance covenants, which must be met on every test date for the life of the loan, from incurrence covenants, which are tested only when the borrower takes an action, such as borrowing more or paying a distribution. Real estate loans usually carry maintenance covenants: debt service coverage, loan to value and sometimes debt yield. Each covenant has three parts that matter as much as the number: the definition of each input, the testing period, and the testing date. Is income the last twelve months actually received, or the next twelve months projected? Is debt service the actual payment or a notional payment at a stressed rate? Is value from a fresh appraisal the lender commissions at your cost, and how often?

A worked example, with hypothetical round numbers. A loan requires coverage of 1.20. Under definition A, income is the last twelve months received; under definition B, it is the next twelve months projected from signed leases. A building that lost a large tenant two months ago shows 1.30 under A, because the tenant's rent is still in the trailing figures, and 1.05 under B. The same building is compliant under one loan and in breach under the other. The definition decided the outcome.

The ladder of consequences

Most loans do not jump straight from compliance to default. They climb a ladder. The first rung is a cash trap, also called a lock-up: if coverage falls below a level above the default level, say 1.25, cash that would have been distributed is held in a lender-controlled account. The second rung is a cash sweep: trapped cash is applied to repay the loan. The third rung is the event of default, often at a lower level, say 1.10 or below 1.0, which lets the lender accelerate the loan and enforce its security. Some loans add a reporting rung: when a covenant weakens, the borrower must provide more frequent information. These levels are commercial practice and are negotiated loan by loan.

Say that out loud now.

Trap, then sweep, then default, and the definitions decide which rung I am on.

Cure rights

A cure right lets the borrower fix a breach before it becomes a default. The most common in real estate is the equity cure: the sponsor deposits cash, which is treated either as extra income for the test or as a prepayment of the loan, bringing the ratio back into line. Lenders limit equity cures: a maximum number over the life of the loan, no consecutive cures, and sometimes a requirement that cure cash prepays debt rather than sitting in an account. A second worked example, hypothetical. A building's coverage is 1.15 against a 1.20 covenant, on 3,000,000 dollars of debt service, so income of 3,450,000 dollars is 150,000 short of the 3,600,000 needed. If the cure counts as income, a 150,000 dollar deposit cures it for that test. If the cure must prepay the loan, the deposit must shrink debt service by enough that 3,450,000 divided by the new debt service equals 1.20, so debt service must fall to 2,875,000 dollars, a reduction of 125,000 dollars a year; at an 8 percent loan constant, that requires prepaying about 1,560,000 dollars. The same breach costs ten times as much to cure depending on the wording.

The clause that has no number

Many loans also contain a material adverse change clause, which lets the lender refuse to fund, or in some cases declare a default, if a material adverse change has occurred in the borrower, the project or sometimes the markets. Its wording varies widely, and courts in different places read such clauses differently. Negotiate to narrow it: limit it to the borrower and the project, exclude general market conditions, and require objective evidence. A trigger with no number is a trigger the other side decides.

Reporting and the compliance certificate

Covenants are tested through documents you deliver. Most loans require a periodic compliance certificate, signed by an officer of the borrower, setting out the covenant calculations and confirming that no default has occurred. Like a draw certificate, it is a statement of fact made by you. A certificate that shows a ratio of 1.21 on figures that were adjusted to reach it is the beginning of a much worse problem than a breach. Build the calculation from the loan's own definitions, keep the working papers, and make sure the person who signs it has the authority recorded in your company's resolutions and has seen the evidence. If a test is likely to be close, tell the lender before the certificate is due, with your plan. A lender who hears early can often agree a waiver; a lender who learns from a certificate rarely wants to.

What to negotiate

Five points. Definitions that match how the asset really earns, with clear treatment of one-off items. Testing on trailing figures for a stabilised asset and on agreed projections during lease-up. A gap between the cash trap level and the default level, so you have time to act. Equity cures that count as income, with a realistic number allowed. And a clear, objective release: trapped cash is released once the ratio has recovered for a stated number of tests. Professional sign-off required: lawyer, as borrower's counsel on the covenant and default provisions.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is signing a loan whose covenant definitions you have not modelled, so your first breach comes as a surprise from the lender's compliance team. The control is to build the lender's exact definitions into your own model and test every case, base, downside and severe, against them before close.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner negotiates the covenant number down by a tenth and ignores the definition, the testing date and the cure. The number is the least important of the four.

Callback

In Week 39, Priya taught the road from term sheet to commitment letter, conditions precedent, covenants and events of default. This lesson is the operating life of those covenants: how they are tested every quarter, and how a ladder of consequences gives you time to act if you have written your own triggers above the lender's.

Recap

Maintenance covenants are tested every period; their definitions, periods and dates matter more than the number. Breaches climb a ladder: trap, sweep, default. Equity cures are limited, and their wording can change the cost tenfold. Narrow any material adverse change clause. Model the lender's definitions before you sign.

Next: Roman, on The Numbers: reverse engineering the break-evens from a coverage of 1.0 and the lender's cash trap.
checklist: I have modelled the lender's exact definitions of income, debt service and value.
I know each covenant's testing period and testing dates.
I know the cash trap, sweep and default levels and the gap between them.
I know how many equity cures I have and whether cure cash counts as income.
I have negotiated an objective release of trapped cash.
I have narrowed any material adverse change clause.
My own triggers sit above the lender's cash trap level.
My lawyer has signed off on the covenant and default provisions.
head: Field checklist
speak: A lender writes its stress test into the loan as covenants. Maintenance covenants, such as debt service coverage and loan to value, are tested every period, and four things decide them: the number, the definition of each input, the testing period and the testing date. A building that just lost a tenant can show 1.30 on trailing income and 1.05 on projected income, so the definition decides whether I am in breach. Breaches climb a ladder: a cash trap holds distributions, a sweep repays the loan, and a default lets the lender enforce. An equity cure lets me fix a breach with cash, but lenders limit the number, and if cure cash must prepay the loan instead of counting as income, the same 150,000 dollar shortfall can cost me about 1,560,000 dollars. Any material adverse change clause should be narrowed, because a trigger with no number is a trigger the other side decides. I model the lender's definitions before I sign.
terms: Maintenance covenant — a financial test the borrower must meet on every test date for the life of the loan.
Cash trap — a loan provision that holds cash otherwise available for distribution in a lender-controlled account when a covenant weakens.
Equity cure — the borrower's right to fix a covenant breach by contributing cash, usually limited in number and form.

hostile.q: We will give you two equity cures, and cure cash must prepay the loan. That is standard. Why are you pushing back?
hostile.a: Because on our numbers, prepayment turns a 150,000 dollar income shortfall into a cure of about 1,560,000 dollars, which is a penalty rather than a cure. I can accept a limit on the number. What I am asking is that the first cure in any twelve months counts as income for that test, and that only a second consecutive cure must prepay. That keeps your protection against a lasting decline and stops a single bad quarter from costing ten times its size.

title: Reverse Engineering the Break-Evens
summary: Start from the failure point, coverage of exactly 1.0, and work backward to the rent, vacancy, operating cost and interest rate that would cause it. Then do the same for the lender's cash trap. All numbers are hypothetical.
body:
A break-even is a stress test run backward. Start from the moment the project fails a test, then solve for how far each assumption would have to move to get there. The answers tell you, in plain units, how much room you really have.

Recall

Q. What is the ladder of consequences in a loan agreement?

A. A cash trap holds distributions, a cash sweep applies trapped cash to the loan, and an event of default lets the lender accelerate and enforce. Levels are commercial practice, negotiated loan by loan.

Q. How do you size a project loan from the coverage covenant?

A. Divide net operating income by the minimum coverage ratio to get maximum debt service, divide by the annuity factor to get the loan, compare with loan to cost and take the smaller.

Q. What does sizing to the binding limit mean?

A. Running every sizing test, such as coverage, loan to value and debt yield, and lending the smallest amount any of them allows.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, "the deal is robust" means nothing to a lender. "Rents can fall 17 percent before we stop covering debt service" means a great deal. Today you reverse engineer: start from the finished outcome, failure, and work backward to the numbers that would cause it. All figures are hypothetical round numbers.

The facts

A stabilised apartment building. Gross potential rent, the rent if every unit were let all year at asking rent, is 6,000,000 dollars. Vacancy and collection loss is 5 percent. Operating expenses are fixed at 1,700,000 dollars. So effective income is 6,000,000 times 0.95, 5,700,000 dollars, and net operating income (NOI) is 5,700,000 less 1,700,000, which is 4,000,000 dollars. The loan is 40,000,000 dollars, floating rate, interest only, currently at 7.5 percent, so debt service is 3,000,000 dollars a year. Coverage is 4,000,000 divided by 3,000,000, about 1.33. The loan has a cash trap at 1.20 and a default at 1.00.

Step 1: the NOI at failure

Coverage of 1.0 means NOI equals debt service: 3,000,000 dollars. NOI can therefore fall by 1,000,000 dollars, or 25 percent, before the project stops covering its debt. That is the master number. Every other break-even is a way of losing that 1,000,000 dollars.

Step 2: the rent break-even

Hold vacancy at 5 percent and expenses at 1,700,000. NOI equals 0.95 times rent less 1,700,000. Set that equal to 3,000,000: 0.95 times rent equals 4,700,000, so rent equals about 4,947,000 dollars. Rent can fall from 6,000,000 to about 4,947,000, about 17.5 percent, before coverage hits 1.0. Notice that a 25 percent fall in NOI needs only a 17.5 percent fall in rent, because expenses do not fall with rent. That is operating leverage working against you.

Say that out loud now.

Fixed costs make NOI fall faster than rent.

Step 3: the vacancy break-even

Hold rent at 6,000,000 and expenses at 1,700,000. NOI equals 6,000,000 times occupancy less 1,700,000. Set equal to 3,000,000: occupancy equals 4,700,000 divided by 6,000,000, about 78.3 percent. Vacancy can rise from 5 percent to about 21.7 percent before failure.

Step 4: the expense and rate break-evens

Expenses: hold income at 5,700,000; NOI of 3,000,000 allows expenses of 2,700,000, a rise of 1,000,000, about 59 percent. Rarely the binding risk on its own, but insurance and property taxes can move fast. Interest rate: hold NOI at 4,000,000; coverage of 1.0 needs debt service of 4,000,000, so the rate can reach 4,000,000 divided by 40,000,000, which is 10 percent, a rise of 2.5 percentage points.

Step 5: the same against the cash trap

Your distributions stop long before default. At the 1.20 trap, NOI must be at least 1.20 times 3,000,000, which is 3,600,000 dollars, so NOI can fall only 10 percent. Rent can fall from 6,000,000 to about 5,579,000, about 7 percent. Vacancy can rise only to about 11.7 percent. And the rate can rise only to 4,000,000 divided by 1.20, about 3,333,000 of debt service, which is 8.33 percent, a rise of less than 0.85 percentage points. That last number deserves a pause: on a floating rate loan, a modest rate rise traps your cash.

Step 6: the table

InputTodayAt cash trap, 1.20At failure, 1.00
NOI4,000,0003,600,000, minus 10 percent3,000,000, minus 25 percent
Gross potential rent6,000,000about 5,579,000, minus 7 percentabout 4,947,000, minus 17.5 percent
Vacancy5 percentabout 11.7 percentabout 21.7 percent
Interest rate7.5 percentabout 8.33 percent10 percent

Each break-even holds every other input constant. All figures are hypothetical, in dollars.

Step 7: combinations

Single break-evens overstate your room, because real trouble moves several inputs at once. Downside: rent 5 percent lower, vacancy 10 percent, rate one point higher. Effective income is 6,000,000 times 0.95 times 0.90, about 5,130,000; NOI about 3,430,000; debt service 40,000,000 times 8.5 percent, 3,400,000; coverage about 1.01. Three moderate moves, none near its own break-even, take you to the edge of failure. Severe: rent 10 percent lower, vacancy 15 percent, rate two points higher. Income about 4,590,000, NOI about 2,890,000, debt service 3,800,000, coverage about 0.76.

Step 8: what the numbers tell you to do

The rate is the closest break-even to the trap. That points to a hedge, an interest rate cap or a swap, which you studied in Week 36, before any work on rent. The combined downside sits at 1.01, so a reserve sized to the severe shortfall, about 910,000 dollars a year, is the second control. And your own triggers belong above 1.20, perhaps at 1.30, so you act before the lender's trap does.

Step 9: check one answer forward

Take the rent break-even and run it forward to prove it. Rent of 4,947,000 dollars times 0.95 is about 4,700,000 of effective income. Less 1,700,000 of expenses gives 3,000,000 of NOI. Divided by 3,000,000 of debt service, coverage is 1.00. The reverse was right. Do the same for the trap: 5,579,000 times 0.95 is 5,300,000, less 1,700,000 is 3,600,000, divided by 3,000,000 is 1.20. A break-even that has not been checked forward is a number you have not yet earned the right to quote.

Step 10: what a rate cap changes

Suppose you buy a cap that limits the rate to 8.5 percent. Debt service can then never exceed 40,000,000 times 8.5 percent, 3,400,000 dollars. The rate break-even against default disappears, because no rate above the cap can raise debt service further. Against the trap, the binding question moves back to income: with debt service at its capped maximum, NOI must stay above 1.20 times 3,400,000, which is 4,080,000 dollars. That is above today's 4,000,000, so at the cap rate the trap would already be triggered. The cap prevents failure; it does not prevent the trap. If distributions matter to your investors, the cap level has to be lower, around 8.33 percent, or the reserve has to cover the gap. Price both before you choose.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is reporting single break-evens as your margin of safety. The control is to report the combined downside beside them, so no one reads 17.5 percent as the room you really have.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner computes break-evens against default and forgets the cash trap. For an investor who needs distributions, the trap is the failure that matters first.

Callback

In Week 43, Roman computed a break-even exchange rate for a cross-border loan. The method is the same for every input: set the test equal to its threshold and solve for the one variable you are moving.

Recap

Start from coverage of 1.0 and work back: NOI can fall 25 percent, rent 17.5, vacancy rise to 21.7 percent, and the rate to 10 percent. Against the 1.20 trap the room roughly halves, and the rate is the nearest danger. Combined moderate moves reach failure faster than any single one.

Next: Roman, on The Room: presenting the stress tests to an investment committee that wants the deal to work.
checklist: I start every break-even from the threshold and solve for one input.
I compute break-evens against both the cash trap and default.
I know my NOI, rent, vacancy, expense and rate break-evens.
I understand that fixed costs make NOI fall faster than rent.
I run a combined downside and severe case beside the single break-evens.
I act first on the break-even closest to the trap.
My own triggers sit above the lender's trap level.
head: Field checklist
speak: A break-even is a stress test run backward. My building earns 4,000,000 dollars of NOI against 3,000,000 of interest-only debt service on a 40,000,000 dollar floating loan at 7.5 percent, so coverage is about 1.33. At failure, coverage of 1.0, NOI can fall 25 percent. Because expenses are fixed, rent needs to fall only 17.5 percent to cause that, vacancy would have to reach about 21.7 percent, and the rate 10 percent. But the lender's cash trap at 1.20 bites much sooner: NOI down 10 percent, rent down 7 percent, vacancy about 11.7 percent, or the rate up less than a point, to about 8.33 percent. And moderate moves together, rent down 5, vacancy at 10 and the rate up a point, take coverage to about 1.01. So I hedge the rate first, hold a reserve sized to the severe shortfall, and set my own triggers above the lender's.
terms: Gross potential rent — the rent a property would earn if every unit were let all year at asking rent.
Operating leverage — the effect of fixed costs that makes net income fall faster, in percentage terms, than revenue.
Interest rate cap — a hedge that pays the borrower when a floating reference rate rises above an agreed level.

hostile.q: You say rents can fall 17.5 percent before you fail. Why is your cash trap only 7 percent away?
hostile.a: Because the 17.5 percent is against default, holding everything else still, and the trap at 1.20 sits much closer. Worse, the nearest threshold is the interest rate: under one point of increase traps our cash. So we are buying a rate cap before closing, holding a reserve sized to the severe shortfall, and our own trigger at 1.30 means you will hear from us, with a plan, before your trap is tested.

title: Presenting the Stress Tests to a Committee That Wants the Deal
summary: An investment committee that likes a deal can make the stress tests feel like disloyalty. Your job is to present the downside without sinking the deal or hiding it. Learn the lines to say, the lines never to say, the question behind the question and how to hold your state when a senior member pushes back.
body:
When a committee wants a deal, the person presenting the downside feels like the only one not on the team. Present it anyway, plainly and with actions attached, because a committee that approves a deal it understands will back you when the severe case arrives.

Recall

Q. In the break-even example, which threshold was closest?

A. The interest rate against the 1.20 cash trap: a rise of under one percentage point, to about 8.33 percent, would trap distributions.

Q. What does the share pledge in a project loan allow?

A. On enforcement, the lender can take the project company itself, keeping its permits and contracts intact, rather than selling the building out of it.

Q. What is an interest rate hedge, in general terms?

A. A contract, such as a cap or a swap, that limits or fixes the interest cost on floating rate debt, so the borrower is protected against rising rates for a price.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, in your own company you will chair these meetings as often as you present to them. Either way, the culture of the room decides whether bad news arrives early or late. If stress tests are treated as disloyalty, people stop running them, and the first sign of trouble arrives as a lender's notice. Presenting the downside well is a leadership skill.

The scene

A hypothetical investment committee: three partners and an outside investor, considering a 50,000,000 dollar apartment development. The team has presented the base case: profit of about 11,500,000 dollars. You present the stress tests. The most senior partner, who sourced the deal, interrupts on your second slide: "We have built in this market for fifteen years. Rents have never fallen 10 percent. Why are we spending time on this?"

The question behind the question

The surface question is about history. The real questions are two. Are you saying my judgment is wrong? And will these numbers kill a deal I have spent months on? If you answer the history question with statistics, you will win the argument and lose the room. Answer the real questions first: you are not questioning his judgment, and the purpose is to approve the deal with its protections, not to stop it.

The lines to say

Start by placing the work. "I am not here to argue against the deal. I am here so that we approve it knowing exactly where it breaks and what we do if we get close."

Then the one number. "The base case works. The closest threshold is the interest rate: under one point of increase traps our distributions under the lender's covenant. That is the risk I would act on first."

Then the combination. "No single input breaks us easily. A moderate downside, rent down 5 percent, vacancy at 10 and rates up a point, all together, takes coverage to about 1.01. That combination is what a mild recession looks like."

Then the actions. "Three proposals: buy a rate cap at closing, hold a reserve of about 1,700,000 dollars sized to the severe shortfall, and adopt written triggers, starting with a review if coverage falls below 1.30. Together they cost about 400,000 dollars a year in cap premium and foregone return, and they turn the severe case from a loss of the building into a bad year."

Say that out loud now.

Here is where it breaks, here is the combination that gets us there, here is what it costs to be ready.

The lines never to say

Never say "I think this deal is too risky" unless that is your recommendation; it turns analysis into opposition. Never say "the model says" as if the model were an authority; the model says what you put in it. Never soften the severe case to keep the peace, and never present it in a tone that suggests you are hoping for it. Never correct the senior partner's history in front of the investor; offer the data afterwards.

When to stay silent

After you state the cost of the protections, stop. The committee needs a moment to weigh 400,000 dollars a year against the severe case. If you fill the silence with reasons, you sound as if you doubt your own proposal. Let the outside investor speak first; investors often ask the question the partners will not.

Holding your state

Being interrupted by the most senior person in the room raises the pulse. Slow your speech, lower your pitch slightly and finish the sentence you were on before answering. Kema's rule from Week 4: a slow outbreath before you reply does more than any argument. Address the person, not the slide.

Worked examples: two endings

Ending one. You defend every number, the senior partner digs in, the committee approves the deal without the cap or the reserve to end the tension. Eighteen months later rates rise, cash is trapped and the investor asks why no one mentioned it. You did; no one heard it.

Ending two. You acknowledge the partner's record, state the single nearest threshold, show the combination, and propose three priced actions. The partner says: "Fine, buy the cap, but the reserve is too big." You answer: "Then let us hold it until coverage has stayed above 1.40 for four quarters, and release it under that rule." The deal is approved with its protections, and the partner has shaped them. That is a better outcome than winning.

The follow-up

Within a day, send the committee one page: the base case, the nearest threshold, the combined downside, the severe case, the three actions with their annual cost, and the triggers with their owners. Send the senior partner, separately, the historical data on rent and rate movements in the market, framed as background for the next deal rather than as a correction. The page becomes part of the approval record. When the market turns, that page is what lets the committee act on its own decision instead of arguing about who said what.

Monthly thread: time and energy on a rotating shift schedule

Stress testing, like any careful analysis, is the work that suffers first when you are tired. On a rotating shift schedule, the hours after a run of night shifts are the worst time to review a model or chair a committee; errors of judgment rise when sleep is short, which is well established in research on shift work. Put your hardest analytical work, and your important meetings, in the hours you are reliably rested, and protect them on the calendar as firmly as a site inspection.

A practitioner habit worth testing: keep a short note of which days and hours your thinking feels sharpest across a full rotation, and schedule decisions there. If sleep, fatigue or caffeine use are becoming a concern, check that with your doctor.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is a committee culture in which stress tests are presented apologetically or not at all, so the deal is approved without its protections. The control is a standing rule: no approval without the downside, the severe case, the break-evens and the triggers on one page.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner presents twenty sensitivities and no recommendation. A committee needs the one nearest threshold, the one combination that matters and the actions, with their cost.

Callback

In Week 28, Sage taught feasibility as a test designed to kill the deal, with go or no-go criteria written in advance. The stress-test presentation is the same discipline later in the life of a deal: criteria and triggers written while the room is calm, so the decision does not depend on who is most senior.

Recap

Answer the question behind the pushback: you are not questioning judgment, you are approving the deal with protections. State the nearest threshold, the combination that matters and three priced actions. Do not soften the severe case, do not correct a senior partner in front of an investor, and stay silent after the cost.

Next: Kema, on Quiz and Recap, with Cole's Auditor's Chair: six questions on stress testing and a hostile read of a stress-test memo.
checklist: I open by saying the purpose is to approve the deal with its protections.
I state the single nearest threshold first.
I show the one combination that matters, as a mild recession.
I propose priced actions, with their annual cost.
I never soften the severe case to keep the peace.
I offer data to a senior partner privately, not in front of an investor.
I stay silent after stating the cost of the protections.
I schedule hard analysis and key meetings in my rested hours.
head: Field checklist
speak: When a committee wants a deal, I present the stress tests as part of approving it, not as opposition. If a senior partner says rents have never fallen, the question behind the question is whether I doubt his judgment and whether I will kill the deal. So I answer that first: I am here so we approve it knowing where it breaks. Then one number, the nearest threshold: under one point of rate increase traps our distributions. Then one combination: rent down 5, vacancy at 10, rates up a point, and coverage is about 1.01, which is what a mild recession looks like. Then three priced actions: a rate cap, a reserve of about 1,700,000 dollars and written triggers, costing about 400,000 dollars a year. Then I stop talking. I never soften the severe case, and I never correct a senior partner's history in front of an investor. A deal approved with its protections is better than winning the argument.
terms: Investment committee — the group that approves or rejects investments on behalf of a firm or fund.
Nearest threshold — the break-even that the project is closest to, and therefore the first risk to act on.
Release rule — a written condition under which a reserve or trapped cash is released, such as coverage above a level for a set period.

hostile.q: Your reserve and cap cost us 400,000 dollars a year for a scenario that has not happened in this market in fifteen years. Why should we pay it?
hostile.a: Because fifteen years is shorter than this loan's life plus our hold period, and the nearest threshold is a rate rise of under one point, which has happened many times in that period, even if rents have not fallen. The cost is about 3.5 percent of our base case profit a year. Without it, a mild recession traps our cash and a severe one can cost us the building. I am also proposing a release rule, so the reserve comes back to us once coverage has stayed above 1.40 for four quarters.

role: Chief of staff and learning coach
title: Week 44 Review: Stress Tests, Break-Evens and Triggers
summary: Six questions test the week: the four tools, why combinations matter, expected outcome versus survival, how covenants and cures work, the break-even method and Rule 44. Cole's Auditor's Chair reads a hypothetical stress-test memo as a hostile auditor would, and a two-minute boardroom drill closes the week.
body:
This week came down to one sentence: know where the deal breaks, test the combinations that actually happen together, size your reserves to the severe case, and write down what you will do before you need to do it.

Recall

Q. In the committee meeting, what should you do immediately after stating the cost of the protections?

A. Stop talking, and let the committee, ideally the outside investor, respond first.

Q. What is the recourse spectrum in project finance?

A. The range from full recourse to pure non-recourse; most project loans are limited recourse, with full support during construction released at a completion test, and carve-outs throughout.

Q. What is the difference between loan to value and loan to cost?

A. Loan to value divides the loan by the property's appraised value; loan to cost divides it by the total cost of the project. Construction lenders often test both.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, stress testing is where your operations background is an advantage: you already think in thresholds, alarms and procedures. If you can answer these six questions without notes, you can bring that discipline to every deal and every lender. Answer each aloud before reading the answer.

The six questions

Question 1. Name the four stress-testing tools and the question each answers.

Answer: Sensitivities, shown as a tornado chart, answer which input matters most. Break-evens answer how far an input can move before a test fails. Scenarios answer what happens when several move together. Triggers answer what you will do when one starts to move.

Question 2. Why can single-variable tests mislead?

Answer: Because real trouble moves correlated inputs together, rent, vacancy, rates and refinancing, so a deal that survives each move alone can fail the combination.

Question 3. What is the difference between the expected outcome and the severe case?

Answer: The expected outcome weights scenarios by probability and tells you whether a deal is worth doing. The severe case tells you whether you can survive it, and sizes reserves and equity.

Question 4. Describe the ladder of consequences and the equity cure.

Answer: A cash trap holds distributions, a sweep repays debt, and a default lets the lender enforce. An equity cure lets the sponsor fix a breach with cash; whether that cash counts as income or must prepay the loan can change the cost of a cure tenfold.

Question 5. How do you compute a break-even?

Answer: Set the test equal to its threshold, such as coverage of 1.0 or the cash trap level, hold the other inputs constant, and solve for the one input you are moving. Then report the combined downside beside it.

Question 6. What is Rule 44?

Answer: Test the plan against a severe case that moves price, credit and refinancing together, not one variable at a time, and write down in advance the trigger and the action for each, because the severe case arrives as a combination.

Say that out loud now.

Recap of the week

Roman framed the four tools: sensitivities, break-evens, scenarios and triggers. Ford and Roman took Dubai World's 2009 standstill, where price, buyer payments and refinancing failed together, giving Rule 44. Sage separated expected outcome from survival and sized reserves to the severe case. LEX read covenants, cash traps and cures. Roman reverse engineered the break-evens from coverage of 1.0 and from the cash trap. Roman then presented the stress tests to a committee that wanted the deal.

Cole's Auditor's Chair

Week 44 is a fourth week, so the Red Pen becomes Cole's Auditor's Chair: read this hypothetical stress-test memo as a hostile auditor would. Find the defects before reading on.

Stress Test Summary. The project was tested for rent minus 5 percent, vacancy plus 3 points and interest rates plus 0.5 points. In every case coverage remains above 1.20, so the project is robust. The ranges reflect management's view of the market. No severe case was run, as a fall of that size is considered highly unlikely by the sponsor. Break-even rent is 17.5 percent below budget, providing a substantial margin of safety. Triggers will be developed if conditions deteriorate. The analysis was prepared by the deal team.

The defects. First, each input was tested alone; there is no combined case, so "in every case coverage remains above 1.20" says nothing about a downturn. Second, the ranges are narrow and were set by management's view, not by history or the lender's assumptions, which an auditor reads as ranges chosen to pass. Third, no severe case was run, on the sponsor's own judgment that it is unlikely; Rule 44 exists because that judgment is exactly what fails. Fourth, the break-even rent is measured against default, not against the cash trap, and quoted as a margin of safety without the combined downside beside it. Fifth, triggers "will be developed if conditions deteriorate," which means after they are needed; a trigger written in a crisis is a reaction, not a plan. Sixth, the analysis was prepared and reviewed by the team that wants the deal, with no independent check.

Then the auditor asks for evidence, and the list is your real lesson. For the ranges, the historical data and the lender's base assumptions. For the cases, the combined downside and severe scenarios, built around a single cause. For the break-evens, both thresholds, the cash trap and default. For the triggers, the written list with owners and actions, approved by the board. For independence, the name of the reviewer and what they checked. A stress test that cannot produce these in an hour was built to reassure.

The boardroom drill

Explain the week in two minutes, as if to a new investor who asks: "How do I know this deal will not blow up?" Then compare with this model.

Model answer: "You cannot know that, and neither can we, so we show you where it breaks. Our base case earns a healthy profit. Our coverage today is about 1.33. Net operating income can fall 25 percent before we stop covering debt, but the lender's cash trap sits much closer, and the nearest threshold is the interest rate: under one point of increase traps distributions. A mild recession, with rent, vacancy and rates all moving moderately, takes coverage to about 1.01. So we buy a rate cap at closing, hold a reserve sized to the severe case's shortfall for eighteen months, and work to written triggers set above the lender's: if coverage falls below 1.30, we review spending and leasing and inform the lender before its test. The deal is worth doing on expected terms, and those protections mean the severe case is a bad year, not the end of the project."

Score your answer. Did you refuse to promise that it would not blow up? Did you give the nearest threshold and one combination? Did you name the actions and their purpose? Did you finish inside two minutes? If not, record it again tomorrow.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk this week is a stress test designed to reassure rather than to find the break. The control is ranges set before the model is run, a combined severe case, both thresholds and an independent reviewer.

The beginner's mistake

Treating stress testing as a chart for the lender rather than an operating plan for yourself. The triggers are the part that protects you.

Callback

In Week 43, Roman built a currency stress with a severe case and a break-even rate. This week generalised it: every input that can move, currency, rent, rates or refinancing, gets a threshold, a combination and a written action.

Recap

Four tools: sensitivities, break-evens, scenarios and triggers. Combinations break deals that single tests pass. Expected outcome judges the deal; the severe case sizes the reserve. Covenants climb a ladder, and their definitions and cures matter more than their numbers. Rule 44 makes the severe case a combination with a written plan.

head: The six questions
speak: This week, stress testing. Four tools. Sensitivities, shown as a tornado chart, rank the inputs that matter most. Break-evens show how far one input can move before a test fails: set the test equal to its threshold and solve. Scenarios move inputs together in base, downside and severe cases, because real trouble is a combination. And triggers turn the test into action: a threshold, a pre-agreed response and an owner. The expected outcome tells me whether a deal is worth doing; the severe case tells me whether I can survive it, and I size reserves to it. Lenders write their own triggers as covenants, with a ladder from cash trap to sweep to default, and the definitions and cure rights matter more than the numbers. Dubai World in 2009 showed price, buyer payments and refinancing failing together. Rule 44: test the severe case as a combination, and write the trigger and action for each in advance.
terms: Stress test — an analysis of how a plan performs when its assumptions are wrong, singly and in combination.
Reverse stress test — starting from failure and working out which combination of events would cause it.
Scenario — a coherent story in which every input is set to fit one cause, such as a recession or a credit crunch.

hostile.q: Your memo says the deal is robust because every test stays above 1.20. Did you test them together?
hostile.a: That earlier memo did not, and it should have. Run together, a moderate rise in vacancy, a small fall in rent and a one-point rate rise take coverage to about 1.01, and the severe case to about 0.76. So we have revised the plan: a rate cap at closing, a reserve sized to eighteen months of the severe shortfall, and written triggers above the lender's cash trap. An independent reviewer has checked the ranges, and I will send you the revised page today.
